project_requirements.title: What the call wants
project_requirements.question: What must the project address, develop and achieve?

cards.title: Central object
cards.question: What is the principal thing the project must develop?
cards.answer:
An innovation that secures the future supply of strategic or critical raw materials, such as copper, aluminium or rare earths, by processing, recovering, reusing or replacing them.
The materials are those on the lists in annexes I and II of the EU Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA, the EU law on secure supply of critical raw materials). The innovation must be applicable in the energy or digital transition, or in the defence or high-tech sector, and reach a first application in the Netherlands within ten years of the start.
cards.sources:
Staatscourant 2026, 31380 (wijziging RNES en ROES 2026 voor EKOO) · Artikel I, Bijlage 4.2.1 Onderdeel D, innovatiethema 4
EKOO: Kritieke grondstoffen (RVO scheme page) · Waarvoor krijgt u subsidie?; Veelgestelde vragen

cards.title: Scope
cards.question: Which activities fall within the funding opportunity's scope?
cards.answer:
Research and development on processing, recovery, reuse or substitution of listed raw materials; primary mining and projects not mainly about these materials are excluded.
In scope:
- Enabling processing (turning ores, minerals or waste into pure metals, alloys or other usable forms), recovery or reuse of strategic or critical raw materials, as the CRMA defines these terms.
- Using a substitute that adds to the circularity of a product, process or service.
- Strategic raw materials include aluminium, copper, gallium, germanium, battery-grade graphite, lithium, nickel and manganese, cobalt, platinum-group metals, silicon metal, titanium, tungsten and rare earths for permanent magnets; the critical list adds others such as magnesium, boron, helium and vanadium.
- Eligible project types: industrial research, experimental development or both.
Excluded: primary extraction; techniques usable only for primary raw materials from mining; projects not mainly about these materials (they belong in the general circular-economy theme); large consortia (MOOI scheme); pilots and demonstrations (DEI+ scheme); fundamental research.
cards.sources:

cards.title: Problem
cards.question: What type of problem or need must justify the project, and where must it originate?
cards.answer:
The project must address the uncertain supply of raw materials that the energy transition, digital transition, defence or high-tech industry depend on.
The need is societal and industrial: demand for these materials is rising fast while extra production is hard, and many are rarely reused, so future supply is uncertain. The model project plan asks for the problem, research questions, technical and non-technical challenges such as regulation, why the problem matters and who owns it.

cards.title: Deliverables
cards.question: Which concrete outputs must the project produce?
cards.answer:
A concrete result towards the new processing, recovery, reuse or substitution solution, such as a design, model, installation or report, plus a public summary.
The model project plan asks for the concrete result (for example an installation, design, model or report), the development needed for it and how the knowledge feeds follow-up steps towards scale-up and market introduction. Each work package must state its result. Non-confidential knowledge must be published in a report after the project, and RVO and Energy Innovation NL publish a summary of funded projects.

cards.title: Impact
cards.question: Which wider system outcomes and impacts must the project support?
cards.answer:
The project must make the supply of strategic and critical raw materials more secure, and show this is applicable in the energy or digital transition, defence or high-tech.
The model project plan asks how the project improves supply security of critical raw materials and other sustainability effects, the yearly repetition potential in the Dutch market in tonnes of primary non-renewable raw materials or tonnes of CO2, the share reached within ten years, and how it reduces Dutch dependence on scarce foreign raw materials.

cards.title: After the project
cards.question: How must the result be replicated, taken up and kept in use after the project?
cards.answer:
The result must lead to a first application in the Netherlands within ten years, with a credible route to market and public sharing of non-confidential knowledge.
- First application: a demonstration in an operational environment within ten years of the start; large-scale roll-out is not required.
- Wider use: the project plan must describe the business case for producer and end user, scale-up potential, follow-up steps, who takes them and the time to market introduction.
- Knowledge sharing: knowledge transfer is a compulsory but unfunded part of the project; non-confidential knowledge must be published after the project, and publications must mention the Ministry's subsidy.
- Evaluation: participants must help RVO spread results and evaluate effects on request.

cards.title: Number of partners
cards.question: What is the permitted or required consortium size?
cards.answer:
At least two parties working together, one of which must be a company; the scheme sets no maximum, but large consortia are steered elsewhere.
The subsidy goes to participants in a samenwerkingsverband (a collaboration in which each party works at its own cost and risk). It must include at least one onderneming (company). The scheme is meant for projects that are not, or not yet, taken up by a large consortium: large collaborations and large innovation projects must use the MOOI scheme (Missiegedreven Onderzoek, Ontwikkeling en Innovatie, RVO's scheme for large mission-driven consortia) instead. Hired parties do not count as partners.

cards.title: Partner composition
cards.question: Which types of partners must the consortium include?
cards.answer:
Any mix of companies and research organisations, provided at least one company takes part; a research partner is optional.
- Companies: at least one is mandatory. A foreign company may take part and receive funding only through a permanent establishment or subsidiary in the Netherlands, and every partner's work must benefit the Dutch economy.
- Research organisations: optional. RVO counts only universities, universities of applied sciences and the applied research institutes (Deltares, MARIN, NLR, TNO, Wageningen Research) and similar foreign bodies.
- Supply chain: the model project plan says projects that involve the whole chain (developer or producer, supplier and end user) generally score higher on quality, especially when the end user is included.
- Group companies: companies of one group may not form the collaboration on their own; another, unrelated participant is then needed.

cards.title: Distribution of work
cards.question: How must work and budget be distributed among partners?
cards.answer:
Partners must contribute roughly equally, in money and in content, and each must work at its own cost and risk.
- Balance: the scheme page requires all participants to contribute 'financieel en inhoudelijk ongeveer evenveel' (financially and in content roughly equally).
- No full outsourcing: the project may not be fully outsourced, and hiring other parties does not count as real collaboration.
- Real collaboration: without a real collaboration, as tested with RVO's flowchart, the company funding rates drop by 15 percentage points.
- Work packages: the model project plan asks for work packages (or milestones), each labelled as industrial research or experimental development, with the partners involved, go/no-go moments, and categories that match the Excel budget.
- Budget cap: the EUR 500,000 maximum applies to the whole project. If the partners together request more, each partner's grant is cut pro rata.

cards.title: Coordinator
cards.question: What type of organisation may or must act as lead applicant?
cards.answer:
Any participant may act as penvoerder (the lead applicant who submits on behalf of the collaboration); the scheme sets no extra condition on its type.
The penvoerder submits the application and manages it with RVO. The other participants authorise it through a participant form, and a change of penvoerder must be authorised again by every participant. A holding company that does no project work may only act as an intermediary that submits for a group company.

project_requirements.title: TenneT's position
project_requirements.question: What is TenneT's position within the consortium?

cards.title: Coordinate
cards.question: Can TenneT apply or coordinate, and under which conditions?
cards.answer:
Yes, TenneT TSO B.V. could act as penvoerder (lead applicant), as nothing in the scheme limits that role to a type of company.
TenneT would then submit the application for the whole collaboration through RVO's portal with eHerkenning at level eH3 (the Dutch business login for government services), collect the authorisations of the other participants and handle progress reports and changes. It would still need at least one other participant, because a collaboration of group companies alone is not allowed.

cards.title: Participate
cards.question: Can TenneT take part without receiving funding?
cards.answer:
Yes. TenneT could take part without funding, either by doing its own work at its own cost and risk or by contributing money or equipment.
RNES article 4.2.5 lets a collaboration include parties that do project work for their own account and risk without receiving subsidy, or that only help finance the project. RVO's FAQ adds that a participant can also join in kind, for example by making machines and equipment available. A party that is hired and paid to do work is a third party, not a participant.
cards.sources:
Regeling nationale EZ-, LVVN- en KGG-subsidies (wetten.overheid.nl) · Titel 4.2 · Artikelen 4.2.2–4.2.6 · Artikel 4.2.5

cards.title: Receive funding
cards.question: Can TenneT receive funding, and which funding rate or cost rules apply?
cards.answer:
Yes, as a large company at up to 40% of eligible costs, within a EUR 500,000 cap for the whole project.
- Large company (such as TenneT TSO B.V.): 40% of eligible costs for industrial research (research to gain new knowledge for new products, processes or services) or experimental development (building and testing a new product, process or service).
- Without a real collaboration, as tested with RVO's flowchart: 25% (40% minus 15 percentage points).
The grant is state aid under article 25 of the AGVV (the EU General Block Exemption Regulation). TenneT must therefore finance at least 60% of its eligible costs, plus any costs that are not eligible, itself, and it may not finance its own share from the part of the grant calculated with the EUR 80 fixed hourly rate. Because the EUR 500,000 cap is shared, TenneT's grant also depends on what the other partners request.

cards.title: TenneT's likely contribution
cards.question: What contribution would make TenneT credible and useful within the project?
cards.answer:
TenneT could contribute decommissioned cables, conductors and other grid equipment as a source of copper and aluminium, plus its requirements as a future buyer of substitute materials.
This is our interpretation. Copper and aluminium are on the strategic list and the energy transition is a named application area, so recovering and reusing material from old grid assets, or developing substitutes in grid components, fits the theme. A recycler or manufacturer would develop the technology; TenneT could supply material streams, data on volumes and composition, and the end-user business case, which strengthens the quality score. TenneT's grant would be at most 40% of its own eligible costs.

project_requirements.title: Innovation
project_requirements.question: What type of innovation must the project develop?

cards.title: Innovation threshold
cards.question: Must the project produce genuinely new knowledge or technology, or may it integrate and apply existing solutions?
cards.answer:
The project must develop a new or much-improved product, process or service; routine application of existing solutions does not qualify.
Eligible costs are only those for activities that are 'nieuw, creatief, onzeker en systematisch' (new, creative, uncertain and systematic) and lead to transferable and reproducible results. The ranking rewards projects that go further beyond the international state of research or technology, and a possible breakthrough technology scores higher than an incremental innovation.

cards.title: Innovation object
cards.question: In what must the project innovate?
cards.answer:
Technology: new or improved processing, recovery or reuse techniques, or a substitute material that makes a product, process or service more circular.
The scheme names only these technological routes; unlike the general circular-economy theme, it does not mention research on consumer behaviour or business models.

cards.title: Development stages
cards.question: Which development stages must the project cover?
cards.answer:
Only industrial research and experimental development, or a combination; fundamental research, pilots and demonstrations are excluded.
An EKOO project is defined as industrial research or experimental development 'en niet primair uit een pilot of demonstratie' (and not mainly a pilot or demonstration). Pilots and demonstrations go to the DEI+ scheme (Demonstratie Energie- en Klimaatinnovatie), fundamental research to NWO, NWA or PPS Innovatie. Each work package must be labelled as one of the two stages, which also sets its funding rate.
cards.sources:

cards.title: Maturity
cards.question: Which maturity level is expected at the start and end of the project?
cards.answer:
No TRL (Technology Readiness Level) is set; the work must sit between research and first application, which must follow within ten years of the project start.
First application means demonstrating the solution in an operational environment, not yet large-scale roll-out. Since pilots and demonstrations are excluded from the project itself, the project ends before that operational demonstration.

project_requirements.title: Work
project_requirements.question: Which activities or work structure must the project cover?

cards.title: Demonstration
cards.question: Where and under which conditions must the solution be demonstrated?
cards.answer:
No demonstration is required or funded within the project; demonstration in an operational environment comes afterwards, as the first application within ten years.
Projects that are mainly a pilot or demonstration are excluded and steered to the DEI+ scheme. The project may build and test prototypes as part of experimental development, but its main activity must be research and development.

cards.title: Integration
cards.question: How must the activities fit together and with existing systems?
cards.answer:
The project must be one coherent research and development plan carried out jointly by the partners, not a set of outsourced tasks.
The model project plan asks for work packages that group logically connected activities, each with its partners, results and go/no-go moments. The project may not be fully outsourced, and the work must lead towards a concrete product, process or service whose developer takes part in the project.

cards.title: Evidence
cards.question: What must the demonstration prove?
cards.answer:
The application must quantify the expected gain in raw-material supply security and the chance of market success, rather than show test results.
- Repetition potential: yearly potential in the Dutch market in tonnes of primary non-renewable raw materials or tonnes of CO2, and the share expected within ten years.
- Feasibility: the project must be technically and economically feasible, with the working of the technology well substantiated.
- Market success: a substantiated chance of success in the Dutch market, plus a SWOT analysis (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats).
- Side effects: any ecological side effects or negative sustainability effects must be described.

cards.title: User participation
cards.question: How must users take part in the project?
cards.answer:
User involvement is not mandatory, but the model project plan says projects that include the end user generally score higher on quality.
The project plan must also describe the business case for the end user: the target users, why they would choose the product, the non-technological barriers to their use and, where relevant, their payback time.

funding_timing_submission.title: Funding
funding_timing_submission.question: How much funding can the project receive?

cards.title: Funding envelope
cards.answer:
A tender with a budget of EUR 1.85 million and a grant of at most EUR 500,000 per project, shared by all partners.
- Total project size: not capped. At the lowest company rate of 40%, the EUR 500,000 cap covers a project of about EUR 1.25 million in eligible costs; with more research-organisation work, the same cap covers a smaller project.
- Grant request: up to EUR 500,000 per project for all participants together; requests above that are cut pro rata.
- Funding form: a cost-based subsidy, calculated over eligible costs and settled after the project against actual costs.

cards.title: Funding rate and co-financing
cards.answer:
Rates depend on the type and size of each participant; every partner must have its own share fully financed when the application is submitted.
- Research organisation, non-economic activities: 80%
- Small company: 60%
- Medium-sized company: 50%
- Large company: 40%
- Without real collaboration: company rates fall by 15 percentage points.
- Co-financing conditions: each participant finances the part of its costs not covered by the grant itself or through other investors; this may be subject to the grant being awarded.
- Evidence required: per participant, proof of how its own share is financed, such as a bank or investor statement, an annual report or annual accounts. Insufficient proof leads to rejection.

cards.title: Budget constraints
cards.answer:
Only research and development costs under EU state-aid rules are eligible, and several common cost types are excluded.
- Eligible costs: costs needed to carry out the industrial research and experimental development, under the RVO subsidy rules (Subsidiespelregels) of the Ministry of Economic Affairs.
- Excluded costs: costs of activities that were already subsidised; knowledge-transfer activities, which are compulsory but not funded; project management not directly linked to the research work; costs made or committed before the application was submitted.
- Overheads: staff costs may be claimed with a fixed hourly rate of EUR 80; the own share may not be financed from the grant calculated with that rate.
- Subcontracting: allowed as costs of third parties, but the project may not be fully outsourced.

cards.title: Cash flow and financial exposure
cards.answer:
RVO pays advances during the project and sets the final grant only after the project, against actual costs.
- Payment model: advances paid evenly over the project with a linear budget, or per quarter in which costs fall with a milestone budget; the applicant chooses in the project plan.
- Financial reporting or audit: an annual progress report for projects longer than 12 months; at the end, a request to set the final grant, with a board statement for grants of EUR 25,000–125,000 or an auditor's statement for grants from EUR 125,000, plus a final report.

funding_timing_submission.title: Timing
funding_timing_submission.question: What timing should the proposal submission and project follow?

cards.title: Application route
cards.answer:
One stage: a complete application through RVO's online portal between 22 October 2026, 09:00 and 3 December 2026, 17:00.
- Stage 1 — Full application: by 3 December 2026, 17:00. The penvoerder (lead applicant) submits the application form with the model project plan, the model budget and the participants' authorisations, logging in with eHerkenning level eH3 (allow about two weeks to obtain it). Any collaboration that meets the conditions may apply; there is no pre-proposal.

cards.title: Project window
cards.answer:
At most two years, starting within six months of the grant decision and never before the application is submitted.
- Maximum duration: 24 months.
- Required start: within 6 months after the subsidiebeschikking (grant decision letter).
- Eligible-cost period: from the submission of the application; no work, commitments or costs are allowed before that, even if not yet paid.
- First application: the innovation must reach first application in the Netherlands within ten years of the project start.

cards.title: Decision and contracting
cards.answer:
RVO ranks all applications after the window closes and decides within 13 weeks, which it may extend once by 13 weeks.
- Funding decision: about 13 weeks after 3 December 2026, so around early March 2027, or up to 26 weeks if extended (indicative, worked out from the stated term).
- Grant agreement: there is no separate contract; the subsidiebeschikking (grant decision letter) sets the payments and obligations.
- Conditions before starting: if a research organisation takes part, a signed cooperation agreement on costs, risks, results and intellectual property is required before the project starts.

funding_timing_submission.title: Application
funding_timing_submission.question: Mandatory information to include in the application

cards.title: Mandatory submission package — pass/fail
cards.answer:
The application form plus the RVO model project plan, the model budget and proof that no participant is a company in difficulty.
- Application form: RVO's online form, submitted by the penvoerder with eHerkenning eH3.
- Project plan: the Model projectplan EKOO Kritieke grondstoffen, at most 25 pages, readable on its own.
- Budget: the Model begroting EKOO (Excel), with work-package categories matching the project plan.
- Partner documents: each participant's authorisation of the penvoerder; for each company the completed decision scheme and signed declaration that it is not an onderneming in moeilijkheden (a company in financial difficulty under EU rules); proof of financing of each participant's own share.
- On request: RVO may ask for the consolidated annual accounts and organisation chart of the companies.

cards.title: Evaluation and selection — scored or ranked
cards.answer:
A tender: independent experts score four criteria, and the best-ranked projects are funded until the budget runs out.
- Evaluation criteria: contribution to the theme's aims; chance of success in the Dutch market and society; novelty against the international state of the art and strengthening of the Dutch knowledge position; quality (approach, risks, feasibility, partners and efficient use of resources).
- Thresholds: 1 to 5 points per criterion; an application with fewer than 3 points on any criterion is rejected.
- Weighting: none stated; the total points decide the ranking.
- Ranking rules: no grant for a project ranked lower than a similar project, and no grant for a project similar to one already funded under this title.

cards.title: Conditional and exceptional requirements
cards.answer:
Three situations change the rules: a company in financial difficulty, a research partner, and a collaboration that is not real.
- Exception — company in difficulty: it can still receive de minimis aid (small aid allowed outside the state-aid rules) of at most EUR 300,000 over three years, and must add a de minimis declaration.
- Conditional — research organisation taking part: a signed cooperation agreement before the project starts, with rules on costs, risks, results and intellectual property, so that no indirect aid flows to the companies.
- Conditional — no real collaboration: company rates fall by 15 percentage points.
- Recommended: RVO advises contacting KIA CE (the Knowledge and Innovation Agenda Circular Economy) via tender@kia-ce.nl for help building a collaboration.
